summary.text: An electric battery is a source of electric power made of one or more electrochemical cells with external connections for powering devices.
A battery converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy, and its redox reaction can happen only when electrons move through the external circuit.
Primary batteries are used once and discarded, while secondary ones are rechargeable because reverse current can restore the original electrodes.

facts.label: Voltaic pile
facts.value: Built and described by Volta in 1800

facts.label: Term 'battery'
facts.value: First used by Benjamin Franklin in 1749

facts.label: Daniell cell
facts.value: The first practical source of electricity

items.prompt: A battery is powering a flashlight. Which terminal do the electrons leave from?

options.label: The negative terminal
The positive terminal
Both terminals equally
Neither, since electrons stay inside

items.explain: The terminal marked negative is the source of electrons, which flow through the external circuit to the positive terminal.

items.prompt: A battery sits unconnected on a shelf and its chemicals do not run down. Why?

options.label: The chemicals stay inert until the battery is shaken
The reaction can occur only when electrons move through the external circuit
Cold air blocks the electrolyte from moving
The reaction is already finished before sale

items.explain: Batteries are designed so that the energetically favorable redox reaction can occur only when electrons move through the external part of the circuit.

items.prompt: A phone's battery can be recharged, but a flashlight's alkaline cell cannot. What explains the difference?

options.label: The phone battery has no chemicals that react at all
The alkaline cell is simply too large to take a charge
The phone battery keeps its electrodes frozen in place
Reverse current restores rechargeable electrodes, but disposable ones change for good

items.explain: Primary batteries change their electrode materials irreversibly during discharge. Secondary batteries can have the original composition restored by reverse current.

items.prompt: Batteries store less energy per kilogram than gasoline. What partly makes up for this in cars?

options.label: Batteries are always lighter than a fuel tank
Electric cars never need to recharge
Electric motors convert energy to mechanical work more efficiently
Batteries release more heat per kilogram

items.explain: Batteries have much lower specific energy than common fuels like gasoline. In automobiles this is somewhat offset by the higher efficiency of electric motors compared to combustion engines.

items.prompt: Volta saw corrosion at his pile's electrodes as a mere nuisance. What did Faraday show about it?

options.label: It is an unavoidable consequence of how the cells operate
It came from faulty brine-soaked paper disks
It proved the pile was an inexhaustible source of energy
It happened only in dry cells

items.explain: Faraday showed in 1834 that the corrosion effects were an unavoidable consequence of the cells' operation, not a mere nuisance.

items.prompt: Why did replacing the liquid electrolyte with a paste make portable devices practical?

options.label: Paste cells produced a much larger steady current
Liquid wet cells could leak, spill and break, but paste cells avoided that
Wet cells were cheaper but needed a pump
Paste cells could be recharged in minutes

items.explain: Wet cells used liquid electrolytes that leaked and spilled, and glass jars made them fragile, so they were unsuitable for portable appliances. Dry cells with a paste made portable devices practical.
